Invited speakers

Hendrik Hamann

Stony Brook University and Brookhaven National Laboratory

Quo vadis - Grid Foundation Models

Abstract

The growing complexity of electric power systems, driven by renewable energy integration, distributed energy resources, and increasingly dynamic operating conditions, calls for new approaches to grid modeling, analysis, and control. While artificial intelligence and machine learning have demonstrated significant promise across individual power system applications, most existing approaches remain task-specific, system-dependent, and limited in their ability to generalize across different networks and operating conditions.

This talk explores the emerging concept of Grid Foundation Models: large-scale, general-purpose AI models that learn transferable representations of power systems from heterogeneous data, network topology, physical models, and operational experience. We will discuss how advances in foundation models, graph-based learning, and physics-informed AI could enable a shift from narrowly optimized solutions toward adaptable models capable of supporting diverse tasks, including power flow estimation, contingency analysis, stability assessment, forecasting, and operational decision support.

Particular attention will be given to the challenges that distinguish grid foundation models from foundation models in other domains, including the need to respect physical laws, capture network dependencies, generalize across grid topologies and scales, and provide trustworthy predictions under changing operating conditions. We will conclude with a perspective on the research opportunities and foundational advances needed to develop scalable, physically grounded, and reliable AI models for the next generation of power systems.

Biography

Dr. Hamann is the Chief AI Scientist at Brookhaven National Laboratory for Innovation, Science and Security and a Professor at Stony Brook University. Dr. Hamann spent two decades at IBM Research, most recently as Chief Science Officer for IBM Research at the T.J. Watson Research Center. His technical work centered on AI for science. He helped develop a new generation of AI foundation models, which are massive, physics-informed AI systems that learn from and emulate the complexity of natural and engineered environments. He now spearheads the development of AI foundation models for the electric grid, designed to improve resilience and accelerate grid modernization. Dr. Hamann, a Fellow of the American Physical Society, authored over 260 scientific papers and holds more than 180 patents. His contributions have earned him honors, including the American Institute of Physics Prize for Industrial Applications of Physics and the Cozzarelli Prize of the National Academy of Sciences.

Weiwei Yang

Asemic.ai; formerly Microsoft Research

From GridSFM to Asemic: Foundation Models for Feasible Grid Decisions

Abstract

AI has a power grid problem. The power grid has a compute problem. Data centers are arriving faster than transmission lines can be built, so the fastest new capacity is whatever the existing grid can already carry. Finding it is the hard part. AC optimal power flow is nonconvex on its own; siting and switching add discrete choices on top. Each solve is slow, and the search is combinatorial.

Asemic builds physics foundation models to break this compute bottleneck. We start from GridSFM, the first foundation model for the power grid, which showed that one set of weights can learn AC optimal power flow across various grids. We extend it toward what grid decisions need: utility-scale networks and post-fault dynamics, not just steady state. This talk follows the path from curating public data into realistic grid topologies to building models that respect the physics by design. Then we put them to work on the Texas grid and ask three questions: how much new load can the existing wires carry, what does that do to everyone’s electricity bill, and what happens when something breaks?

Biography

Weiwei is the co-founder of Asemic.ai, where she builds foundation models for engineered systems to power civilization, starting with the electric grid. Previously, as a senior director at Microsoft Research, she led the development and open-source release of GridSFM, a foundation model that generalized across diverse power-grid topologies. That work reflects her broader focus at the intersection of AI, physics, and critical infrastructure: creating models that capture the structure and constraints of real engineering systems. At Asemic, she is turning this vision into practical technology that makes the infrastructure society depends on faster, more adaptive, and more resilient under pressure.

Christine Chen

The University of British Columbia

AI for control and operation of modern power grids: opportunities and challenges

Abstract

The increasingly complex, uncertain, and dynamic nature of modern power grids poses unprecedented challenges for ensuring system reliability and security. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers powerful new capabilities for learning system behaviours, extracting insights from large-scale data, and supporting real-time decision-making. Yet, at the heart of power system analysis lies a simple relationship: I = YV. Drawing examples from various application settings, the fundamental law of physics provides the lens through which this talk explores the opportunities and limitations of AI in power system control and operation. We conclude with a forward- and backward-looking perspective on the evolving role of models, physics, and innovation in shaping future power grids.

Biography

Christine Chen is an Associate Professor with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and an Associate Director of the Clean Energy Research Centre at The University of British Columbia. Her research interests include power system modelling, control, and operation. She received the B.A.Sc. degree in engineering science from the University of Toronto and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Her work has been recognized with a Best Paper Award from the IEEE Transactions on Energy Conversion, an IEEE Power and Energy Society Prize Paper Award, and a "Best of the Best" Prize Conference Paper Award at the IEEE Power and Energy Society General Meeting. Christine serves or has served on the editorial boards of the IEEE Transactions on Power Systems, the IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, and the IEEE Transactions on Energy Conversion.

Luis Piloto

Google DeepMind

Accelerating Power System Optimization with Machine Learning

Abstract

Congestion is a growing challenge in modern transmission power grids. Phase-shifting transformers (PSTs) offer a cost-effective means to redirect power flows and mitigate overloads, but determining their optimal discrete tap settings under AC physics requires solving a computationally demanding mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP). In this talk, I will present CANOS-PST, a Graph Neural Network for fast, AC-accurate congestion management via PST tap optimization that embeds a differentiable power flow solver enforcing AC power balance by construction. On synthetic grids across multiple scales, CANOS-PST produces near-optimal solutions in milliseconds with batched GPU scaling, making it well-suited for both time-sensitive operational decisions and large-scale multi-scenario planning studies.

Biography

Luis Piloto is a Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind focusing on machine learning for power grid optimization. He has a Ph.D. in neuroscience from Princeton, where he studied sleep and memory using neuroimaging as well as intuitive physics and developmental psychology using neural networks. Before that he received a Bachelor's degree in Cognitive Science and Computer Science at Rutgers University. Prior to that, he was a software developer in the travel industry.

Pascal Van Hentenryck

Georgia Tech and Gurobi Optimization

Reliable AI for Power Systems Optimization

Biography

Pascal Van Hentenryck is the A. Russell Chandler III Chair and Professor in ISyE at Georgia Tech, the director of the US National Science Foundation (NSF) AI Institute for Advances in Optimization (AI4OPT), and the head of the AI Innovation lab at Gurobi Optimization. He was a professor of Computer Science at Brown University for over 20 years and led the optimization research group at National ICT Australia. Van Hentenryck is a pioneer of constraint programming, and designed several optimization systems that have been in commercial use for over 20 years. He has published 6 books and over 400 articles. He is a fellow of AAAI and INFORMS, and the recipient of two honorary degrees and numerous awards. His current research focuses on fusing AI and optimization for engineering with primary applications in energy systems, supply chains, manufacturing, and health care.

Bernardo Costa

School of Applied Mathematics, Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV EMAp)

Can we detect multistage strategies in the Energy market?

Abstract

The Brazilian energy market has several mechanisms for pricing, but most dealing with system operation are cost-based.  Historically, hydro generation was dominant, state-owned, and priced by substitute (thermal and deficit costs) at minimum long-term operation costs; recently, a risk-aversion parameter was introduced to further protect against extreme dry scenarios.  However, the energy mix in Brazil has substantially changed, with introduction of wind and solar energy that have introduced new challenges for pricing, making especially relevant intra-day price fluctuations.  There have been proponents of a price/bid-based market for the Brazilian system, but the reality is still that hydro power has a significant market share and even more so in ancillary services such as frequency, ramping, etc.  This poses significant challenges in market design, as hydro strategies involve state, uncertainty and risk-aversion, and therefore can be performed in very long-term horizons that might be difficult to detect (or prove) by the system operator or regulator.  I will discuss some proposals, and mathematical limitations, around those issues.

Biography

Bernardo Costa is a professor of mathematics at the School of Applied Mathematics, Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV), Brazil. His current research focuses on convex optimization, though he also worked with complex analysis and stochastic processes. He is particularly interested in multistage stochastic optimization and applications to the energy sector, having collaborated for 10 years with the Brazilian ISO in several research projects including modeling and algorithms for efficient operations planning.

Nando Ochoa

University of Melbourne, Australia

Learning Where No Electrical Model Exists: Voltage Calculations from Real Smart Meter Data

Abstract

Most machine learning for power grids assumes an electrical model exists, so training data can be generated by running power flows. While that might hold at transmission and medium voltage levels, it fails in low voltage (LV) networks, the residential infrastructure where rooftop solar, batteries and electric vehicles connect, because distribution companies rarely have accurate electrical models. This talk takes a different starting point. Using real smart meter data from Victoria, Australia, it shows that machine learning can capture the physics of three-phase LV networks and calculate voltages for any what-if scenario, with no electrical model and no power flow simulations. This enables fast, accurate assessment of what more of these technologies would do to voltages, without ever building an electrical model.

Biography

Luis (Nando) Ochoa is a Professor of Smart Grids and Power Systems at The University of Melbourne. His research focuses on electricity distribution networks, particularly the integration of distributed energy resources and the use of data-driven and AI techniques in low voltage networks, where electrical models are often poor or missing altogether. Working with Australian distribution companies, his team has developed electrical model-free approaches that calculate voltages and operating envelopes directly from real smart meter measurements. He is an IEEE PES Distinguished Lecturer and previously held academic roles at the University of Manchester and the University of Edinburgh.

Invited panelists

Priya Donti

MIT

Biography

Priya Donti is an Assistant Professor and the Silverman (1968) Family Career Development Professor at MIT EECS and LIDS. Her research focuses on safe and robust machine learning for high-renewables power grids. Priya is also a co-founder and Chair of Climate Change AI, a global nonprofit initiative to catalyze impactful work at the intersection of climate change and machine learning. She received her Ph.D. in Computer Science and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University. She was recognized in MIT Technology Review's 2021 list of 35 Innovators Under 35, Vox's 2023 Future Perfect 50, and the 2025 TIME100 AI list, and is a recipient of the Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Early Career Fellowship, the ACM SIGEnergy Doctoral Dissertation Award, and best paper honorable mentions at ICML and ACM e-Energy.

Arnaud Zinflou

Hydro-Québec

Biography

Arnaud Zinflou is a Principal Research Scientist at the Hydro-Québec Research Institute (IREQ), where he leads research and development activities in artificial intelligence for power systems and industrial applications. His work spans time-series forecasting, computer vision, representation learning, uncertainty quantification, and trustworthy AI. At Hydro-Québec, he contributes to the development and deployment of AI solutions supporting grid operations, asset management, infrastructure inspection, and decision support. His recent research focuses on foundation and world models for time series, self-supervised learning, and operationally reliable AI systems for critical infrastructure. He is the author or co-author of more than 50 scientific papers, 7 book chapters, and 3 patents, and has been an IEEE Senior Member since 2015.
